title: Act III, Scene IV

teacherSummary.text: At the state banquet a Murderer tells Macbeth that Banquo is dead but Fleance escaped. When Macbeth wishes Banquo were present, Banquo's ghost sits in his place, seen only by Macbeth, who cries 'Thou canst not say I did it.' Lady Macbeth explains it as a fit he has had since youth and scolds him ('Are you a man?'). The ghost returns; the feast breaks up in disorder. Afterwards Macbeth says 'blood will have blood,' notes that Macduff refused to come, and resolves to visit the Witches: 'I am in blood stepp'd in so far…'

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Act III, Scene IV (where it begins, turns and ends) and its symbolism shape the reader's understanding of the ghost at the banquet. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Act III, Scene IV suggests about the ghost at the banquet. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the scene's symbolism and characterization), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how William Shakespeare uses symbolism in Act III, Scene IV to complicate the reader's understanding of the ghost at the banquet. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Act III, Scene IV within its historical and literary context and argue how the scene's treatment of the ghost at the banquet responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Act III, Scene IV alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the scene's handling of the ghost at the banquet follows or bends those conventions, using the symbolism as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Act III, Scene IV and its treatment of the ghost at the banquet. State your method, show what it reveals in the scene's symbolism and characterization, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Act III, Scene IV as evidence for a larger claim about the ghost at the banquet in Macbeth. Connect close reading of the scene to the whole play, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Act III, Scene IV as a hinge in the play's larger treatment of the ghost at the banquet. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Macbeth.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
